title: Obadiah
subtitle: a short, sharp word against the brother who stood by
lead: Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament: one chapter, twenty-one verses. Its target is Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin. When Jerusalem fell, Edom stood aside, gloated, looted and cut off the people running for their lives. The book says the LORD saw it, that Edom's cliff-top pride will be brought down, and that the same thing will happen to every nation that treats a neighbor this way.

Then it turns to hope. The "day of the LORD" is near, Zion will have survivors, Jacob will burn like fire and Esau will be like straw, and the lost lands and scattered exiles will be gathered. It ends in one line: "royal power will belong to the LORD." The first nine verses closely resemble Jeremiah 49:7-22, and how the two are linked is a puzzle that scholars have worked on for two centuries.
facts: "Obadiah," a name meaning "servant of the LORD." The book gives no father, home town, king or date. Tradition ties him to Ahab's steward or to an Edomite convert; the evidence does not.

Uncertain. The commonest view: shortly after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC (verses 10-14), with verses 15-21 perhaps added later in the Persian period. An older view: the 800s BC, when Edom revolted under Jehoram.
On the commonest dating: Judah after the Babylonian conquest, and the exiles. Edom lay on the high plateau southeast of the Dead Sea.
A prophetic oracle against a foreign nation, a charge speech, a day-of-the-LORD poem and a promise of restoration
1 chapter, 21 verses; the shortest book in the Old Testament
The English and Hebrew verse numbers are the same (21 verses).
Fourth of the Twelve in the Hebrew Bible, after Amos; fifth in the Greek order, after Joel (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah)
authorship: A prophet named Obadiah, who spoke against Edom. Jewish tradition (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b) is reported to identify him with Ahab's steward and to call him a convert from Edom; Jerome says Jewish teachers of his day did the same. Christian commentators have generally treated him as an Old Testament prophet of uncertain date.

The book is anonymous, and the name may have been attached later. Most date verses 1-14 after 586 BC and see verses 15-21 as a later addition or expansion; some see the whole as a unit. The relation to Jeremiah 49 (borrowing either way, or a shared source) is open.

The Targum reads Sepharad as Spain; the medieval commentators and the Talmud (Bavli Yoma 10a) read Zarephath as France. Edom, as Esau's line, often stands for Rome and, later, for the Christian world.

audience.to: On the commonest dating, the people of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC: survivors in the land, refugees, and exiles, who knew Edom as a brother nation and had seen it join their enemies. Edom is addressed as "you," but oracles against nations were spoken or written for the people of God, not delivered to the nation named.
audience.why: On the commonest dating, the book answers a question the survivors were asking: did anyone see what Edom did, and will anything be done? The book says yes. The LORD saw (verses 10-14), will bring Edom down (verses 1-9), and will repay all nations for their deeds (verse 15). Then it gives them a future: survivors on Zion, the land taken back, and the LORD's rule (verses 17-21). Knowing that the first hearers were wounded and powerless explains the book's tone: it is a word of comfort and justice for the victims, and it leaves vengeance to the LORD instead of putting a sword in their hands.
views: The commonest view. The survivors and exiles of Judah, with verses 15-21 read as hope for the exiles.
The older view: the kingdom of Judah in Jehoram's day, after Edom's revolt (2 Kings 8:20-22) and the raid on Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 21:16-17).
The Twelve as a collection, read by Judeans in a small province, with Edom's power already shrinking and the Nabataeans rising.

outline: The report and the call to the nations; Edom's pride in its rock fortress
Edom plundered, betrayed by allies, its wise men lost
The charge: violence to a brother, and eight "do nots"
The day of the LORD for all the nations, and the cup
Zion's survivors, Jacob and Esau, the lands and the exiles, and the LORD's rule

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Edom's betrayal when Jerusalem fell in 586 BC (the commonest dating), with the earlier option of Edom's revolt under Jehoram labeled; Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22, Ezekiel 25 and 35, Malachi 1:2-5; Edom's decline, the Nabataeans and Idumea.

lenses.name: Critical scholarship
lenses.desc: The relation of verses 1-9 to Jeremiah 49:7-22; whether verses 1-14 and 15-21 are one book or later additions; the book's place in the Twelve (catchwords with Amos 9:12 and Joel 3:19); the Greek and the scrolls 4QXIIg and Mur 88.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Edom as Esau and later Rome in the rabbinic tradition; Obadiah as an Edomite convert (Bavli Sanhedrin 39b); the reading of Sepharad as Spain and Zarephath as France; the haftarah for Vayishlach in Sephardic custom. This site has not checked the Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimhi or midrash passages on Obadiah, so none is attributed a view.

lenses.name: Christian tradition
lenses.desc: Jerome's report on Obadiah and Ahab's steward; Esau and Edom as a figure of the world or the church's enemies; the "rescuers" of verse 21 read of the apostles or Christ (a labeled reception); the warning that anti-Edom language was sometimes turned on Jews. This site has not checked the Cyril, Theodoret, Calvin or Luther commentaries on Obadiah, so none is attributed a view.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: The day of the LORD for all nations (verse 15), the return of the exiles (verses 17-20) and "royal power will belong to the LORD" (verse 21), read by different traditions as fulfilled, partly fulfilled or future.

sections.b:
Read it in three movements. Verses 1-9 are the sentence against Edom: the LORD calls the nations, takes away its cliff-top safety, lets its allies betray it. Verses 10-14 give the reason: the violence done to a brother, spelled out in eight "do nots." Verses 15-21 widen the view: a day of the LORD for all nations, and a future for Zion. The word "day" ties the book together: it comes ten times in verses 11-14 for the day Jerusalem fell, and then once for "the day of the LORD" (verse 15).

Pay attention to "brother." Edom is not accused of being foreign but of being kin. That is what makes the accusation hurt, and it explains why Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 35 all return to it.

Edom was a small kingdom on a high plateau southeast of the Dead Sea, with copper mines, caravan roads and stronghold towns (Bozrah, Teman, Sela). Israel and Edom were bound by kinship (Genesis 25-36; Deuteronomy 23:7) and by wars (Numbers 20:14-21; 2 Samuel 8; 2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 28:17). Under Assyria and then Babylon, Edom was a vassal state. After 586 BC Arab tribes moved in and Edomites drifted west into the Negev; the Nabataeans took over the old Edomite land and built Petra. The Edomites of the south of Judea were called Idumeans; John Hyrcanus conquered them and forced circumcision, and Herod the Great came from them (Josephus, Antiquities 13.9.1; 14.1). Obadiah does not predict Herod. Malachi 1:2-5 is the other prophetic comment on Edom's fate.

Obadiah 1-9 and Jeremiah 49:7-22 share lines and images (the call to the nations, the proud height, the thieves and grape gatherers, the loss of Edom's wise). They are not copies: the order differs, some verses are in one book only, and the wording varies. The three explanations are that Obadiah used Jeremiah, that Jeremiah used Obadiah, or that both used an older Edom oracle. See the table on the chapter page. The Plain English Translation follows Jeremiah's English only where the Hebrew is the same.

sections.h: The text, the scrolls and the Greek
sections.b: The Plain English Translation translates the Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex). I read the Greek in Swete's edition and the Dead Sea Scrolls in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription (ETCBC) as printed by the site's tool. Two scrolls contain Obadiah: 4QXIIg (4Q82), which keeps most of verses 1-15 in part and often only as restored letters, and Mur 88, the Minor Prophets scroll from Wadi Murabba'at, which has all 21 verses, with much of verses 16-21 restored. Both agree with the Masoretic Text in almost every visible word. The few differences are in spelling, apart from 4Q82 at verse 4 (a verb form), Mur 88's shorter spelling of "his gate" at verse 11, and Mur 88's yod in the word for "their property" at verse 17. The printout marks 4Q82's verb at verse 15 as differing from the Masoretic Text in vav and yod only, and I rest no reading on it. The Greek has different readings at verses 1 ("I heard"; "siege" for "envoy"), 5, 7 (no "your bread"), 9-10 (the word "slaughter"), 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21 ("to take vengeance"). The variants list these.

The Hebrew Bible counts the twelve short prophets as one scroll, ordered Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah. Amos 9:12 ends with taking "the remnant of Edom" and Obadiah begins with Edom; Joel's day of the LORD and its "valley" for the nations (Joel 3) come two books earlier, and Joel 3:19 names Edom too. The Greek order puts Obadiah after Joel. Scholars who study the Twelve as a collection (Nogalski and others) see these links as deliberate; others doubt that the Twelve were planned as one book.

Vengeance. The book speaks of the LORD's repayment (verse 15), not of Judah's sword. Readers differ on how to hear this (see the card at verse 15). Fairness to Edom. The book gives one side, the injured; Edomite voices are not preserved. Misuse. From the early church on, "Esau" and "Edom" were turned into labels for Jews in some Christian preaching, and in Jewish tradition Edom became a label for Rome and later the Christian world. Neither use is in the text, and the first has fed contempt and violence against Jews. This site reads Obadiah first as a word about a real nation.

spec.title: Brought down, then going up
spec.body: My own observation. The verb "bring down" (yarad) is used twice of Edom's fall in verses 3-4 ("Who will lower me to the ground?"; "from there I will bring you down"). The last verse turns the direction: rescuers "will go up" ('alah) Mount Zion. The book is built as a reversal of height: Edom on its cliffs is brought down, and the low and scattered go up. The word is not unusual for its time; the pairing as a frame for the book is my suggestion, and I know of no commentator who states it this way.

prompts: A drawing sketched onto an aged scroll in ink and ochre: a great eagle's nest set impossibly high on a red cliff among painted stars, with a tiny human city carved into the rock below, in the style of an ancient manuscript mixed with cave drawing and modern line art, soft hand-drawn edges, no hard rectangle.

A scroll sketch in black ink and red earth pigment: a fork in a narrow mountain road, refugees with bundles hurrying along one branch and shadowy figures standing at the junction, loose, sketchy lines like a cave painting, soft torn edges, no hard rectangle.

A scroll drawing in charcoal and orange wash: a bright flame spreading through a field of pale stubble under a darkening sky, in the style of an ancient manuscript with a modern graphic feel, soft hand-drawn edges, no hard rectangle.
reading: A full, careful commentary with the Hebrew, the text-critical questions and the relation to Jeremiah 49.
John Barton, Joel and Obadiah (Old Testament Library)
A clear, shorter commentary with a good account of the dating.
Ehud Ben Zvi, A Historical-Critical Study of the Book of Obadiah
A detailed study of the book's date, structure and relation to other prophets.

The history and archaeology of Edom.
